evidenceAudit.scope: Hepatic encephalopathy (HE) in adults with cirrhosis or acute-on-chronic liver failure (ACLF) in India: West Haven grading, finding and treating precipitants, lactulose, rifaximin, airway protection, nutrition and secondary prophylaxis, built on the ICMR Acute Liver Failure / ACLF STW (July 2020) and the AASLD/EASL HE guideline (2014).
findings: Lactulose 20–30 mL every 6 hours titrated to 3–4 stools/day, rifaximin 400 mg three times daily, airway protection in grade 3–4 coma, mannitol only in acute liver failure without renal failure, ceftriaxone 1 g twice daily for spontaneous bacterial peritonitis (SBP), and investigations checked against the ICMR ALF/ACLF STW (July 2020).

West Haven grades, precipitants (Table 3), ammonia not needed for diagnosis (recommendation 9), lactulose 25 mL every 1–2 hours until 2 soft stools then titrate to 2–3/day (recommendation 19), rifaximin add-on and secondary prophylaxis (recommendations 20, 25, 26), BCAA and IV LOLA as options, and nutrition targets (recommendations 30–32) checked against AASLD/EASL 2014.
unverifiedSections: The ICMR rifaximin dose (400 mg three times daily) is used; the AASLD/EASL extract did not state a dose.
IV L-ornithine L-aspartate (LOLA) and branched-chain amino acids (BCAA) are options for non-responders (AASLD/EASL) but no doses were in the opened sources.
Paediatric HE is outside the scope of the cited sources.
The ascitic neutrophil cut-off of 250/mm³ for SBP is standard practice; it was not in the opened ICMR workflow.
Drug cautions, contraindications and renal or hepatic adjustment lines without a source tag are general pharmacology statements and need formulary confirmation.

pathophysiology.summary: Hepatic encephalopathy is brain dysfunction caused by liver insufficiency or portosystemic shunting, ranging from subtle cognitive changes (covert HE) to coma. Gut-derived ammonia and other toxins bypass the failing liver, causing astrocyte swelling and altered neurotransmission. Most episodes in cirrhosis are triggered by a precipitant: infection, gastrointestinal bleeding, diuretic overuse, electrolyte disorders or constipation (AASLD/EASL Table 3); correcting it resolves most episodes. Lactulose is the first-line treatment; rifaximin is added to prevent recurrence. Blood ammonia does not diagnose, grade or predict HE (AASLD/EASL recommendation 9).
keyMechanisms: Failing liver and portosystemic shunts let gut-derived ammonia reach the brain.
Astrocytes convert ammonia to glutamine, causing swelling and low-grade cerebral oedema.
Inflammation from infection amplifies ammonia neurotoxicity.
Lactulose acidifies the colon and traps ammonia; rifaximin reduces ammonia-producing bacteria.

symptoms: Lethargy, disorientation to time, personality change (grade 2)
physicalSigns: Signs of the precipitant: fever, melaena, dehydration
redFlags: Gastrointestinal bleeding: see the Upper GI bleeding topic
Fever or abdominal pain: suspect SBP
Focal signs or seizures: look for another cause

differentials.distinguishingFeatures: Alcohol history; ophthalmoplegia or ataxia; give thiamine.
Focal deficit or head injury; computed tomography (CT) head.
Fever, neck stiffness; cultures, lumbar puncture.

diagnosticCriteria.threshold: Trivial lack of awareness, euphoria or anxiety, short attention span, impaired addition or subtraction, altered sleep rhythm; oriented.
Lethargy or apathy, disorientation for time, personality change, inappropriate behaviour, asterixis.
Somnolence to semi-stupor, responsive to stimuli, confusion, gross disorientation.
Bilirubin 5 mg/dL or more and INR 1.5 or more in chronic liver disease; additional organ failure means severe disease.

clinicalManagement.title: Stabilise
actions: Grade 3–4: secure the airway; intubate if needed (ICMR STW).
Check glucose; give dextrose if low (ICMR STW).

clinicalManagement.title: Find and treat precipitants
actions: Look for infection, bleeding, electrolyte disorder, dehydration, constipation and sedatives (AASLD/EASL Table 3).
Diagnostic paracentesis if ascites; treat SBP (ICMR STW).
Stop diuretics and nephrotoxins in kidney injury (ICMR STW).
Gastrointestinal bleeding: treat as in the Upper GI bleeding topic.

clinicalManagement.title: Start lactulose
actions: Oral or nasogastric lactulose (see medicines); titrate to 2–3 soft stools a day (AASLD/EASL) or 3–4 (ICMR STW).
Avoid overuse: dehydration and hypernatraemia worsen HE (AASLD/EASL).

clinicalManagement.title: Not improving
actions: Re-examine for another cause and missed precipitant (AASLD/EASL).
Options: rifaximin add-on, oral BCAA or IV LOLA (AASLD/EASL recommendations 21–22).
ACLF with organ failure: refer to a higher centre or intensive care unit (ICU) (ICMR STW).

clinicalManagement.title: Secondary prophylaxis
actions: Lactulose after the first episode (AASLD/EASL recommendation 25).
Add rifaximin after a second episode (AASLD/EASL recommendation 26).
Recurrent intractable HE with liver failure: refer for liver transplant assessment (AASLD/EASL recommendation 13).

patientEducation: Take lactulose daily; aim for 2–3 soft stools.
Family: watch for confusion or sleepiness and seek care early.
Do not drive while recovering from overt HE.
lifestyleAndDiet: Energy 35–40 kcal/kg and protein 1.2–1.5 g/kg a day; do not restrict protein (AASLD/EASL recommendations 30–31).
Small frequent meals and a late-night snack (recommendation 32).

dischargeCriteria: On lactulose with stool target understood
nonClinicalManagement.followUpPlan: Hepatology review in 1–2 weeks; continue prophylaxis; transplant assessment if recurrent.
